description: Equipo de estudiantes de una escuela secundaria técnica, conformado por personas que ansían enfrentar nuevos desafíos, investigar, diseñar soluciones y poner a prueba sus conocimientos.
summary: We developed a 3D space mission simulator. Initially, we planned to create an interactive control panel, but during the event, this concept evolved into an interactive 3D program featuring a space rocket. It is designed to train astronauts for potential fires, drawing on real-world space missions and related NASA experiments. We believe this is significant, as it could help future spacecraft crew members understand how to respond to hazardous situations, such as fires.
details: Our project is an interactive 3D simulator that teaches how fires start, behave and are prevented inside a spacecraft cabin in microgravity. Users play five scenarios based on NASA research and real incidents (cold flame, normal flame, Apollo 1, Mir and Apollo 13) and adjust oxygen level, cabin pressure, equipment load, CO₂ suppressant, gravity and a blocked escape route. The model computes the oxygen partial pressure (O₂ × (1 − CO₂) × pressure) and compares it with the ignition temperature of the equipment: if the equipment overheats while there is enough oxygen, a flame appears, and pyrolysis particles trigger an early warning first. The status moves from normal to caution to critical, with a police-style siren and a spoken “problem detected” alert, and the user can switch between the cabin view, a 3D risk map and a first-person view inside the cabin, where they move around and put on oxygen masks. Timed missions ask the user to return the cabin to a safe state before time runs out. The main benefit is learning by doing: users experience how small changes in oxygen or pressure turn a safe cabin into a deadly one, safely, for free and in any browser on computers and phones, with no installation or account, while real incidents and NASA research ground each scenario and the timed missions train quick decision-making under pressure. We expect it to raise awareness of spacecraft fire safety among students, space enthusiasts and the general public, since fire is one of the most dangerous risks in space and matters even more on missions far from Earth, where escape and resupply are not possible; because it is open, lightweight and easy to share by link, teachers and outreach programs can reuse it, and it can be extended with real NASA data and more scenarios. We built it with HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript, using Three.js (WebGL) for the 3D scene, the Web Audio API for the siren and the Web Speech API for the voice alert, with Git and GitHub for version control, Vercel for automatic deployment and Claude, an AI assistant, to support development; we tested on a standard computer and smartphones, and no special hardware is needed. The project is creative because it turns scientific data into a playable control room instead of a static explanation, uses famous disasters like Apollo 1 and Mir as missions, makes a counterintuitive phenomenon (cold flames in microgravity) something users can explore, and adds design details such as solar panels that retract while the rocket moves and deploy when it stops, a first-person view inside the cabin, and an alarm that combines a siren with a voice alert. Our team considered scientific grounding (NASA experiments such as Saffire, FLEX and ACME and the Apollo 204 report, simplified for clarity and presented as an educational model rather than an engineering tool), accessibility (no installation or registration, responsive design for phones and touch controls), performance (lighter 3D rendering on phones so it runs smoothly), clarity (color-coded alert levels, an in-app manual and references, and sound cues that convey urgency) and maintainability (separate HTML, CSS and JavaScript files, a GitHub repository and automatic deployment, so updates are easy).
